**Nasir Gebelli** ([Persian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_language "Persian language"): ناصر جبلی, also **Nasser Gebelli**, born 1957) is an [Iranian-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian-American "Iranian-American")[programmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programmer "Programmer") and [video game designer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_designer "Video game designer") usually credited in his games as simply **Nasir**. He became known in the early 1980s for programming [action games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_game "Action game") for [Apple II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II "Apple II"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-barton-1) such as _[Space Eggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Eggs "Space Eggs")_ (a clone of _[Moon Cresta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon\_Cresta "Moon Cresta")_). These were initially published by [Sirius Software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sirius_Software "Sirius Software"), then he started his own company, Gebelli Software.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Several of the games he wrote for Gebelli Software were 3D [space combat simulators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_combat_simulator "Space combat simulator") for the Apple II.

From the late 1980s to the early 1990s, Gebelli developed [home console](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_console "Home console") games for Square. He programmed the first three _[Final Fantasy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final\_Fantasy "Final Fantasy")_ games,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-friendz-2) the [Famicom 3D System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Famicom_3D_System "Famicom 3D System") title _[Rad Racer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rad\_Racer "Rad Racer")_, _[3-D WorldRunner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3-D\_WorldRunner "3-D WorldRunner")_, and _[Secret of Mana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secret\_of\_Mana "Secret of Mana")_.

## Early life and career (1957–1985)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nasir_Gebelli&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and career (1957–1985)")]

Gebelli was born in [Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran") in 1957. Because of his family relationship with the Iranian royal family of the [Pahlavi dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pahlavi_dynasty "Pahlavi dynasty"), he migrated to the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") to avoid the 1979 [Iranian Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_Revolution "Iranian Revolution") and study [computer science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_science "Computer science").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-3) He was inspired by [golden-age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_age_of_arcade_video_games "Golden age of arcade video games")[arcade video games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arcade_video_game "Arcade video game"), such as _[Space Invaders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Invaders "Space Invaders")_.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-levy-4) Gebelli's first project for the [Apple II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II "Apple II") was _EasyDraw_, a logo and character creation program he used for his later games. He then began programming video games in either 1978 or 1979.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-nextgen-5)

### Sirius software

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nasir_Gebelli&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Sirius software")]

As a college student, he demonstrated a slideshow program he wrote at a computer store to the store's owner Jerry Jewell.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-levy-4) In 1980, he joined a new company founded by Jewell and Terry Bradley, [Sirius Software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sirius_Software "Sirius Software").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-levy-4) Gebelli's first game was _Both Barrels_.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-nextgen-5)

Within a year, Gebelli programmed twelve games.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-levy-4) He claimed to have written the code in his head and then quickly entered it before forgetting the details.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-interview-6) His action games were well-received, and three of his games, _Phantoms Five_, _Cyber Strike_, and _Star Cruiser_, appeared on _Softalk_'s Top Thirty software list in March 1981.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-softalk-7) Six of his games later appeared on _Softalk_'s Top Thirty list in August 1981, with the highest at number three.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-8) His best-selling titles were _[Space Eggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Eggs "Space Eggs")_ and _[Gorgon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorgon\_(video\_game) "Gorgon (video game)")_, which were clones of _[Moon Cresta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon\_Cresta "Moon Cresta")_ and _[Defender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defender\_(1981\_video\_game) "Defender (1981 video game)")_, respectively.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]_[Electronic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic\_Games "Electronic Games")_ referred to Gebelli as "ace designer Nasir" and gave _Gorgon_ a positive review.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-eg198101-9)_[BYTE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byte\_(magazine) "Byte (magazine)")_ assured readers that _Gorgon_ would not disappoint "Nasir Gabelli fans".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-callamaras198112-10)_Gorgon_ sold at least 23,000 copies in a year, making it one of the [best-selling computer games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_best-selling_PC_video_games "List of best-selling PC video games") through June 1982.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-cgw_1982-11) Gebelli's games used [page flipping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Page_flipping "Page flipping"), which eliminated the flickering that early Apple II games experienced.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-levy-4)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-softalk-7)

### Gebelli software

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nasir_Gebelli&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Gebelli software")]

He left Sirius in 1982 to establish his own software company, Gebelli Software, which released its first game that same year.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Entitled _Horizon V_, the game was a [first-person shooter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-person_shooter "First-person shooter") with a [radar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automap "Automap") mechanic. Sirius released the Apple II game _Zenith_ later in 1982, which added the ability for players to rotate their ships. In October 1982, _Arcade Express_ reviewed _Zenith_ and scored it 9 out of 10, stating "celebrated Nasir proves his reputation" with "this visually striking first-person space piloting and shooting" game.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-12) In March 1983, however, _Andromeda_ (fourth place for Atari 8-bit), _Russki Duck_ (tied for sixth for Apple) and _Horizon V_ (tenth place for Apple) received _[Softline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Softline\_(magazine) "Softline (magazine)")_'s Dog of the Year awards "for badness in computer games" based on reader submissions.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-softline198303-13)_Horizon V_ sold 5,000 copies during its first few months on sale in 1982.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-cgw_1982-11)

[IBM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM "IBM") arranged for Gebelli to produce [launch titles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Launch_title "Launch title") for the [IBM PCjr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM_PCjr "IBM PCjr"), announced in late 1983.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-wiswell19840124-14) Gebelli's company was not successful, and the [video game crash of 1983](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_crash_of_1983 "Video game crash of 1983") caused Gebelli Software to close.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Afterward, Gebelli went on an extended vacation traveling the world. When he retired from Apple II development, Gebelli had eight games on _Softalk_'s Apple II best-seller lists, more than any other game designer.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Square (1986–1993)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nasir_Gebelli&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Square (1986–1993)")]

In 1986, Gebelli became interested in developing games again and met with [Doug Carlston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doug_Carlston "Doug Carlston"), his friend and owner of video game developer [Broderbund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broderbund "Broderbund"). Carlston told him about the rise of the [Nintendo Entertainment System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_System "Nintendo Entertainment System") and how he should start creating games for the console. Gebelli was interested, and so Doug offered to fly to [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") with Gebelli and introduce him to his contacts at [Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_(video_game_company) "Square (video game company)"). Gebelli had the opportunity to meet with [Masafumi Miyamoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masafumi_Miyamoto "Masafumi Miyamoto"), founder and president of Square, who decided to hire him. The programmers, especially [Hironobu Sakaguchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hironobu_Sakaguchi "Hironobu Sakaguchi") (a long-time fan of Gebelli's work), were aware of his reputation and were excited to have him join.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-friendz-2)

### Famicom 3D System

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nasir_Gebelli&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Famicom 3D System")]

While at Square, Gebelli programmed the game _Tobidase Daisakusen_ for the [Famicom Disk System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Famicom_Disk_System "Famicom Disk System"), released in the United States in early 1987 as _[3-D WorldRunner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3-D\_WorldRunner "3-D WorldRunner")_ on the [NES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_System "Nintendo Entertainment System").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-nextgen-5)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-WorldRunner-15)_3-D WorldRunner_ was a [pseudo-3D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2.5D "2.5D")[third-person](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third-person_(video_games) "Third-person (video games)")[platform game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platform_game "Platform game") where players move in any forward-scrolling direction and leap over obstacles and chasms.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-nextgen-5) It was also notable for being one of the first [stereoscopic video games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereoscopic_video_game "Stereoscopic video game").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-WorldRunner-15) His second Square project was _Highway Star_ (_[Rad Racer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rad\_Racer "Rad Racer")_ in the U.S.), a stereoscopic 3-D [racing game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racing_video_game "Racing video game") also designed for the _[Famicom 3D System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Famicom\_3D\_System "Famicom 3D System")_ in 1987. According to Sakaguchi, Square initially hired Gebelli for his 3D programming techniques, as seen in _3-D WorldRunner_ and _Rad Racer_.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-hard-17) At the time, Gebelli did not know any [Japanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_language "Japanese language") and had no translator, so it was initially difficult to communicate with Sakaguchi. There were only three staff members working on both games, Gebelli, Sakaguchi, and graphic designer [Kazuko Shibuya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazuko_Shibuya "Kazuko Shibuya"). Both games were commercially successful, selling about 500,000 copies each.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-nextgen-5)

### _Final Fantasy_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nasir_Gebelli&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Final Fantasy")]

Gebelli then teamed up with Sakaguchi, [Nobuo Uematsu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobuo_Uematsu "Nobuo Uematsu") and [Yoshitaka Amano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoshitaka_Amano "Yoshitaka Amano") as part of Square's A-Team to produce _[Final Fantasy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final\_Fantasy\_(video\_game) "Final Fantasy (video game)")_, the first entry in the popular [_Final Fantasy_ series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_Fantasy "Final Fantasy"). A [role-playing video game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Role-playing_video_game "Role-playing video game") released for the NES in 1987 in Japan, it featured several unique features, a [character creation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Character_creation "Character creation") system, the concept of [time travel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_travel "Time travel"), side-view battles and transportation by canoe, boat and airship.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-gspot_finalfhist_a-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-gspot_consolehist_j-19) It also had the first RPG [minigame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minigame "Minigame"), a sliding puzzle added by Gebelli into the game despite its not being part of Square's original game design.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-dengeki-20)

He went on to program _[Final Fantasy II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final\_Fantasy\_II "Final Fantasy II")_, released in 1988, introducing an "emotional storyline, morally ambiguous characters, tragic events". He also made the story "emotionally experienced rather than concluded from gameplay and conversations". The game replaced traditional levels and experience points with a new [activity-based progression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experience_point#Activity-based_progression "Experience point") system that required "gradual development of individual statistics through continuous actions of the same kind". _Final Fantasy II_ also featured [open-ended](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_world "Open world") exploration[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-ff2-21) and an innovative [dialogue system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dialog_tree "Dialog tree") where players use keywords or phrases during conversations with [non-player characters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-player_character "Non-player character").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-FFII-22)

Gebelli went on to program _[Final Fantasy III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final\_Fantasy\_III "Final Fantasy III")_ in 1990, which introduced the [job system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Job_system "Job system"), a character progression engine allowing the changing and combination of [character classes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Character_class "Character class").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-FF3jobs-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-square_ffmanual-24) Midway through the development of both _Final Fantasy II_ and _III_, Gebelli returned to [Sacramento, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento,_California "Sacramento, California") from Japan due to an expired work visa. The rest of the development staff followed him to Sacramento with materials and equipment needed to finish game production.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-25)

### _Secret of Mana_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nasir_Gebelli&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Secret of Mana")]

After completing _Final Fantasy III_, Gebelli took another long vacation and later returned to work on _Seiken Densetsu II_ (released as _[Secret of Mana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secret\_of\_Mana "Secret of Mana")_ in the U.S.), the second entry in the _[Mana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mana\_(series) "Mana (series)")_ series, released in 1993. The game made advances to the [action role-playing game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_role-playing_game "Action role-playing game") genre, including its unique [cooperative multiplayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooperative_video_game "Cooperative video game") gameplay. The team who created the game had worked on the first three Final Fantasy titles: Gebelli, Koichi Ishii, and [Hiromichi Tanaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiromichi_Tanaka "Hiromichi Tanaka"). The team developed _Secret of Mana_ to be a launch title for [Super NES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Nintendo_Entertainment_System "Super Nintendo Entertainment System")'s [CD-ROM add-on](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_NES_CD-ROM "Super NES CD-ROM"). After Sony and Nintendo backed out of making the console, the game was changed to fit in a standard Super NES game pak.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-1up-26)

The game received considerable acclaim[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-EuroGamer-27) for its innovative [pausable real-time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time-keeping_systems_in_games#Pausable_real-time "Time-keeping systems in games") battle system,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-Apple-29) stamina bar,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-30) the "[Ring Command](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radial_menu "Radial menu")" menu system,[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-Apple-29) its innovative cooperative [multiplayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplayer_video_game "Multiplayer video game") gameplay,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-EuroGamer-27)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-NowGamer-31) and the customizable [AI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence") settings for computer-controlled allies.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-32)

## Later life (1994–present)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nasir_Gebelli&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Later life (1994–present)")]

Following _Secret of Mana's_ completion, Gebelli retired with income from Square royalties and travelled the world. In August 1998, he attended an Apple II Reunion in [Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas "Dallas"), Texas, at video game developer [Ion Storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ion_Storm "Ion Storm") offices. There, he met developer and fan [John Romero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Romero "John Romero"), who interviewed him.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-youtube-33)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-interview-6) Gebelli lives in [Sacramento, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento,_California "Sacramento, California"), where he has lived most of his life.

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nasir_Gebelli&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Legacy")]

[John Romero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Romero "John Romero") (_[Wolfenstein 3D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfenstein\_3D "Wolfenstein 3D")_, _[Doom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doom\_(1993\_video\_game) "Doom (1993 video game)")_, _[Quake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quake\_(video\_game) "Quake (video game)")_) credited Gebelli as a significant influence on his career as a game designer.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-youtube-33) He also cited Gebelli as his favorite programmer and a notable inspiration, mentioning his fast action and 3D programming work on games such as _Horizon V_ and _Zenith_.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-barton-1) Gebelli also inspired the careers of other developers, such as Mark Turmell (_[NBA Jam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA\_Jam\_(1993\_video\_game) "NBA Jam (1993 video game)")_, _[Smash TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smash\_TV "Smash TV")_).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-interview-6)[Jordan Mechner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_Mechner "Jordan Mechner") has also credited Gebelli's work on the Apple II as inspiration and as a major influence on the creation of _[Karateka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karateka\_(video\_game) "Karateka (video game)")_ and _[Prince of Persia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince\_of\_Persia "Prince of Persia")_.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-34) Richard Garriott (_[Ultima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultima\_(series) "Ultima (series)")_) also praised Gebelli's ability to craft games that "were really playable and fun!"[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-35)

_[Final Fantasy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final\_Fantasy "Final Fantasy")_ went on to become a major franchise, and [Hironobu Sakaguchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hironobu_Sakaguchi "Hironobu Sakaguchi") went on to become a well-known figure in the game industry. _Final Fantasy_'s side-view battles became the norm for numerous console RPGs.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-gspot_finalfhist_a-18) Developers used _Final Fantasy II_'s [activity-based progression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experience_point#Activity-based_progression "Experience point") system in several later RPG series, such as the _[SaGa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SaGa\_(series) "SaGa (series)"),_[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-RPGFan-Romancing-Saga-36)_[Grandia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandia\_(series) "Grandia (series)"),_[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-37) and _[The Elder Scrolls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Elder\_Scrolls "The Elder Scrolls")_.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]_Final Fantasy III_'s job system became a [recurring element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recurring_elements_in_the_Final_Fantasy_series "Recurring elements in the Final Fantasy series") in the _Final Fantasy_ series. _Secret of Mana_ has also influenced later action RPGs,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-NowGamer-31)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-38) including modern titles such as _[The Temple of Elemental Evil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Temple\_of\_Elemental\_Evil\_(video\_game) "The Temple of Elemental Evil (video game)")_[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-39) and _[Dungeon Siege III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dungeon\_Siege\_III "Dungeon Siege III")_.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_Gebelli#cite_note-NowGamer-31)

_Rad Racer_ and _Final Fantasy_ both contain anti-piracy checks that look for "NASIR" and "PROGRAMMED BY NASIR" respectively in memory.
